texts.profile:
TITLE: Photosynthesis: Light Into Sugar

INTRO: Nothing here is scored; a wrong answer only shows what to look at next. Warm-up from memory: what gas do you breathe out, and what sugar might a plant make? Most people say carbon dioxide and glucose.

SECTION 1 - The Core Reaction
Photosynthesis is the process where plants make glucose, a sugar, from carbon dioxide and water. Light energy from the sun powers the reaction. The arrow chain is: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen. Takeaway: light-powered sugar-making is the core.
EXAMPLE: Try it: In a video game, a plant item takes in carbon dioxide and water and uses light; what sugar does it make? Answer: glucose.

SECTION 2 - Where Light Is Absorbed
Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs the light. It sits in chloroplasts, which are structures inside leaf cells. Photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves because leaf cells hold most of the chloroplasts. Takeaway: chlorophyll in chloroplasts is the light catcher.
EXAMPLE: Try it: In a comic panel, light hits a leaf; which pigment absorbs it? Answer: chlorophyll.

SECTION 3 - Products and By-Product
Oxygen is released as a by-product; the plant does not use it in this reaction. Glucose is the useful product: it stores energy and builds plant material. So the outputs are glucose plus oxygen. Takeaway: glucose is the product; oxygen is the by-product.
EXAMPLE: Try it: A basketball player says the main food-making site is the leaf; is that right? Answer: yes, mainly in the leaves.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A basketball player sketches the photosynthesis play as 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Check that the atoms balance.
  1. Count carbon atoms: the left side has 6 from 6CO2; the right side has 6 in C6H12O6. Carbon balances.
  2. Count hydrogen atoms: the left side has 12 from 6H2O; the right side has 12 in C6H12O6. Hydrogen balances.
  3. Count oxygen atoms: the left side has 6 x 2 + 6 = 18; the right side has 6 in glucose plus 6 x 2 = 12 in 6O2, which is 18. Oxygen balances.
  4. Name the parts: carbon dioxide and water are raw materials, light energy powers the reaction, chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs the light, and oxygen is released as a by-product.
  ANSWER: The play balances: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2, powered by light and absorbed by chlorophyll.

COMMON MISTAKES:
Wrong: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + O2. Why: the oxygen atoms do not balance; the right side has 6 + 2 = 8 oxygen atoms, but the left side has 6 x 2 + 6 = 18. Right: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2.

SUMMARY: Photosynthesis makes glucose from carbon dioxide and water, using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll in chloroplasts, mainly in leaves; oxygen is released as a by-product.

CHECK QUESTIONS:
1. Which pair are the raw materials for photosynthesis? [choices: carbon dioxide and water | glucose and oxygen | oxygen and water | chlorophyll and glucose] -> carbon dioxide and water
2. Name the structure inside a leaf cell where chlorophyll is found. [typed answer] -> chloroplasts
texts.mirror:
TITLE: Photosynthesis: How Plants Make Their Food

INTRO: Plants do not eat food the way you do. They build their own sugar inside their leaves, using air, water and sunlight. That building job is called photosynthesis, and this lesson shows you the rule, then works it through step by step.

SECTION 1 - The recipe: carbon dioxide plus water makes glucose
Rule: plants make their own food, a sugar called glucose (a sweet fuel the plant uses for energy). They build it from two ingredients: carbon dioxide, a gas in the air, and water, which comes up from the roots. This sugar-building job is called photosynthesis. Photo means light and synthesis means putting together, so photosynthesis means putting together using light. Nothing else gets added: just carbon dioxide and water, plus energy you will meet in the next section.
EXAMPLE: Here is the recipe as an arrow chain, with what goes in on the left and what comes out on the right.

carbon dioxide (from the air) + water (from the roots) + light energy  ->  glucose (sugar the plant keeps) + oxygen (given out)

Read the arrow as 'turns into'. Left side: what the plant takes in. Right side: what it makes. In a comic you would draw the sun as an arrow pointing at the leaf, with carbon dioxide arrows going in and an oxygen arrow puffing out.

SECTION 2 - Light energy and chlorophyll
Rule: building glucose takes energy, and the plant does not get that energy from food. It takes light energy from the sun, which is why a plant left in a dark cupboard cannot make glucose for long. The light is caught by chlorophyll, the green stuff that gives leaves their colour. Chlorophyll sits inside chloroplasts, tiny green bags inside leaf cells. Chlorophyll absorbs the light: it soaks the light up and passes that energy into the sugar-building.
EXAMPLE: Chlorophyll works like a player catching a pass. The sun is the passer, chlorophyll is the catcher, and the energy it catches is what drives the sugar-building. Think of the ball as light energy. Miss the catch, and the play stops, just as an unlit plant stops making glucose. A basketball team that never gets the ball cannot score.

SECTION 3 - Oxygen out, and mostly in the leaves
Rule: photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves, because that is where most chloroplasts are and where the light lands. Oxygen is released as a by-product, meaning something made along the way that this job does not need. The plant lets the oxygen out through tiny holes in the leaf. The glucose is used straight away for energy or stored as starch. The roots bring the water, but the sugar factory itself is the leaf.
EXAMPLE: A by-product is the extra stuff you get without asking. When you ink a comic drawing and rub out the pencil lines, the eraser crumbs are a by-product: you did not want them, but you got them anyway. Oxygen is the plant's eraser crumbs: useful to us, not the point of the job.

Try it: A plant makes 2 glucose molecules, and each glucose comes with 6 oxygen molecules released. How many oxygen molecules does it release? Answer: 2 x 6 = 12 oxygen molecules.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A bean plant on a sunny windowsill makes 3 glucose molecules. Each glucose molecule needs 6 carbon dioxide molecules and 6 water molecules, and releases 6 oxygen molecules. Work out what the plant takes in and what it gives out, and say where this happens.
  1. Step 1. Write the rule in arrow form: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen. The left of the arrow is what goes in, the right is what comes out.
  2. Step 2. Carbon dioxide is used at 6 molecules per glucose. So 3 glucose molecules need 3 x 6 = 18 carbon dioxide molecules.
  3. Step 3. Water is also used at 6 molecules per glucose. So 3 x 6 = 18 water molecules are needed.
  4. Step 4. Oxygen is released at 6 molecules per glucose. So 3 x 6 = 18 oxygen molecules are given out.
  5. Step 5. The light energy comes from the sun and is absorbed by chlorophyll inside chloroplasts, and this all happens mainly in the leaves.
  6. Step 6. Check the count matches the rule: 18 carbon dioxide and 18 water go in, 3 glucose and 18 oxygen come out, and nothing appears from nowhere.
  7. Step 7, you finish it: if the plant made 5 glucose molecules instead, the oxygen released would be 5 x 6 = ___ molecules. (Answer: 30.)
  ANSWER: In: 18 carbon dioxide molecules and 18 water molecules, plus light energy from the sun. Out: 3 glucose molecules and 18 oxygen molecules. Place: mainly in the leaves, where chlorophyll in the chloroplasts absorbs the light.

COMMON MISTAKES:
Wrong: Plants get their glucose from the soil, and water carries it up to the leaves. Why: the soil gives water and minerals, which are tiny bits of salt, but not glucose; the glucose is built in the leaf itself. Right: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen, all made in the leaves.
Wrong: 3 glucose needs 3 carbon dioxide, one for each glucose. Why: 3 is far too low; each glucose needs 6 carbon dioxide molecules, so the count is 3 x 6 = 18, not 3. Right: 3 x 6 = 18 carbon dioxide molecules.
Wrong: A leaf takes in carbon dioxide and oxygen, uses light energy, and makes glucose. Why: oxygen is not an ingredient; it is released at the end as a by-product. Right: the leaf takes in carbon dioxide and water, uses light energy, and releases oxygen.

SUMMARY: Plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, using light energy from the sun. Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts of leaves absorbs the light. Oxygen is released as a by-product, and the whole job happens mainly in the leaves.

CHECK QUESTIONS:
1. Hint: look at the left side of the arrow chain in section 1. Which gas does a plant take in to make glucose? [choices: Oxygen | Carbon dioxide | Nitrogen | Water vapour] -> Carbon dioxide
2. Hint: each glucose needs 6 carbon dioxide molecules, so multiply. A plant makes 4 glucose molecules. How many carbon dioxide molecules does it need? (Type the number.) [typed answer] -> 24
3. Hint: check each item on the input side against the rule. A learner writes: 'A leaf takes in carbon dioxide and oxygen, uses light energy, and turns them into glucose.' Which part is wrong, and why? [choices: Nothing is wrong; both gases are used. | Oxygen is not an ingredient; it is released as a by-product. | Light energy is not needed for photosynthesis. | Glucose is made in the roots, not the leaf.] -> Oxygen is not an ingredient; it is released as a by-product.
